newsitem.title: USA: Insurance parts of US bank reform bill draw fire.
newsitem.headline: Insurance parts of US bank reform bill draw fire.

text.p: Both banking and insurance groups on Wednesday criticized the insurance regulation sections of a new congressional proposal to overhaul U.S. financial laws.

House Banking Committee Chairman Jim Leach's latest bank reform measure, released late Tuesday, included a host of compromises designed to gain greater support from insurers without alienating bankers.
But bankers said they preferred insurance provisions in earlier proposals that gave banks greater leeway.
And insurers complained that the bill left too many ambiguities regarding state regulation of bank insurance sales.

The banking committee plans to mark up the legislation on June 17 and dozens of amendments are expected. Leach, Republican of Iowa, told the committee that the draft bill released on Tuesday night could be altered before the mark-up.

For more than a decade, Congress has sought to scrap the 1933 Glass-Steagall Act and reform antiquated U.S. bank laws. But the initiatives have always broken down when the major financial industries were unable to reach a consensus.
Ed Yingling, top lobbyist for the American Bankers Association, said the latest proposal "provides a solid basis for a successful mark-up."

Bankers' "areas of concern," however, include the lack of insurance sales authority for national banks in large cities and towns and a prohibition on insurance underwriting by bank subsidiaries, Yingling said. Under current law, banks can sell insurance in towns of less than 5,000 people.
Insurance groups said they were pleased that Leach did not include expansive language from a Clinton administration proposal on bank insurance sales.

The Supreme Court decided last year that federal bank regulators could, in some circumstances, overrule state insurance regulations. The Clinton plan appeared to expand federal preemption authority, insurance groups charged.

Independent Insurance Agents of America "is pleased that chairman Leach has eliminated the Treasury Department's psuedo-functional regulation language that would have rolled back the states' ability to regulate bank insurance sales," said Robert Rusbuldt, vice president of the trade group.
Nonetheless, Rusbuldt said the bill's new regulatory scheme was insufficient.
Without stronger language on regulation, "the confusion and litigation surrounding state oversight of bank insurance activities will continue unabated," he said.
Rusbuldt also called for stronger consumer protection rules regarding bank insurance sales. The Leach bill included such provisions for bank securities and mutual fund sales but not for insurance.

The draft did not include any language regarding the mixing of banks and commercial firms, one of the most contentious issues in the debate. Leach said he expected members would offer a variety of amendments on that subject.
